summary: Defines the cite-as link relation type, which lets a resource convey a preferred URI for referencing it. This helps when the URI used to access a resource is not the one that should be cited. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A link that says 'if you want to mention this page, please use this address instead', like a book telling you the proper way to cite it.

questions: how to indicate a canonical citation link
what is the cite-as link relation
how do i tell tools to cite me a different way
subtitle: A link relation to convey a preferred URI for permanent reference

tldr.problem: Resources on the web are often accessed at one URI but should be cited with a different, more persistent URI. For example, scholarly articles are accessed via a journal's domain but should be cited via a permanent DOI. Currently, no standard link relation conveys this preference.
tldr.mechanism: The cite-as link relation type lets a web resource include a link indicating that applications should reference it by the link target URI instead of the access URI. The target is preferred for citation, archiving, and discovery.
tldr.outcome: Bookmarking tools, citation managers, search engines, and web archives can now recognize and respect the author's or publisher's preference for how the resource should be cited, reducing link rot and improving reference durability.

facts.label: Placement options
facts.value: HTTP Link header or HTML link element

today: RFC 8574 is Informational and has not been obsoleted. The cite-as link relation is registered with IANA and is ready for use in web applications, digital repositories, scholarly publishers, and any service where users reference resources. Adoption in citation tools and search engines is growing as persistent identifier systems and digital preservation communities recognize the value of this standard.

sections.title: The Problem of Access vs. Reference URIs
sections.content:
When a user accesses a web resource, the URI in the browser's address bar (the access URI) may differ from the URI that should be used to reference or cite that resource (the reference URI). This happens in several scenarios. Persistent identifier systems like DOIs, PURLs, and ARKs are designed to remain stable over time, but they typically redirect to a current access location that may change. A scholar accessing an article via its journal's website needs to cite its DOI. A version control system may serve the latest version of a document at one URI but intend citations to reference the specific version accessed. A person may have multiple profile URIs across social networks but prefer one for reference.

Without a standard way to express this preference, citation tools and search engines risk using the access URI instead of the intended reference URI, undermining the durability of citations and persistent identifier investments.
sections.plainLanguage: The address you see in your browser is where the website lives today, but it might move tomorrow. Some sites want you to use a different address when you mention them to others.

sections.title: Common Use Cases
sections.content:
The RFC describes four main scenarios. Persistent identifiers are issued specifically to remain stable over time (e.g., DOI, PURL, ARK). The access URI may change if the publisher or custodian transfers the resource, but the reference URI remains constant through redirection. Version identifiers occur in systems like Wikipedia and arXiv, where the most recent version is always available at a generic URI, but each version has a distinct versioned URI. Citation policies often prefer the versioned URI to ensure accuracy.

Preferred social identifiers are relevant when a person has multiple profiles (LinkedIn, ORCID, personal website). The person may prefer one for reference because it is more complete or not under a third party's control. Multi-resource publications consist of multiple files or chapters, each accessible at its own URI, but they share an intellectual publication URI that should be cited.
sections.plainLanguage: A book chapter has its own URL but should be cited as part of the book. An article version has a generic page and a timestamped version—which do you cite? Someone has accounts everywhere but wants to be cited one way. A dataset has many files but one DOI.

sections.title: The cite-as Link Relation Type
sections.content:
A link with the cite-as relation type indicates that, for referencing the resource (the link context), use of the URI of the link target is preferred over use of the access URI. This allows a resource to unambiguously declare its preferred reference URI. The link can appear in the HTTP Link header or in HTML <link> elements.

The link target SHOULD support protocol-based access (e.g., it SHOULD be a working HTTP URI), and it SHOULD allow a user agent to follow back to the link context (e.g., via redirects or links) to establish trust. A resource SHOULD provide at most one cite-as link. Applications can use this information when bookmarking, recording citations, archiving, or building discovery indices.
sections.plainLanguage: A website can include a link saying 'the official way to mention this is by this other address'. Bookmark tools and search engines should pay attention to that.

sections.title: How cite-as Differs from Other Link Relations
sections.content:
Several IANA-registered link relation types might seem similar but serve different purposes. The alternate relation indicates content variants (e.g., PDF vs. HTML), not a preferred reference URI. The duplicate relation indicates byte-identical copies (like mirror sites), which do not apply to the citation scenarios. The related relation is too vague to convey the specific semantics needed.

The bookmark relation is the closest in intent but is limited by its HTML5 definition: it applies only to article elements and is excluded from the HTTP Link header, making it unsuitable. The canonical relation is intended for search engine indexing (preferring one version for crawling), not citation. In scholarly publishing, publishers already use canonical to point to the indexed article; using cite-as separately indicates the preferred reference URI (e.g., the DOI), allowing both purposes to be expressed.
sections.plainLanguage: Other link types mean 'this is a copy', 'this is a variant', or 'search engines should index this', but none of them mean 'please cite me this way'.

sections.title: Real-World Examples
sections.content:
A scholarly article on PLOS ONE can include a cite-as link from its current access URI to its DOI. When a reader bookmarks or cites the article, tools that recognize the link will use the DOI, which remains stable even if the journal changes publishers.

arXiv.org could use cite-as to point from the generic preprint URI to the specific version URI (v1, v2, etc.) that the reader accessed. This ensures citations reflect the content the reader actually saw.

A person's home page or FOAF profile can include a cite-as link to their preferred profile URI (e.g., an ORCID). A dataset repository can include cite-as links from each file to the dataset's persistent identifier, so each file correctly attributes the publication.
sections.plainLanguage: An article says 'cite me by my DOI'. A dataset says 'cite me as the whole publication, not as individual files'. A preprint says 'cite the version you saw, not the generic page'.
